description: We're merging 20+ years of MODIS and VIIRS data into one burn calendar app with early warnings.
summary:
A fire officer in Cordoba or Punjab wants to know two things: is this month's burning unusual, and what usually comes next? NASA's satellites have watched these places since 2000, but the record cannot answer this today. In 2012 a sharper sensor, VIIRS, joined the older MODIS, and the raw count of fire hotspots jumps about five times overnight. The jump is the camera, not the fire.

Fire Census rebuilds 24 years of NASA FIRMS hotspots into one burning calendar in which 2005 and 2025 mean the same thing. From 2012 it counts only the fires strong enough for the older sensor to see, and scales them by one number for each calendar month. The free web app covers four study areas in Argentina and India. Inside them it shows the calendar for any area a user draws, names or types, ranks the current month against every earlier year, and lets the user download the data and charts.

We wrote down ten checks before opening the data, and we publish every result, including the ones that failed.
details: WHAT IT DOES Fire Census is a free website that shows how much burning happened in an area in every month from 2000 to today. Open the link and the first line answers the question a fire officer asks first: is this month's burning unusual here? For Punjab and Haryana, with data up to 13 November 2026, the first 13 days of November rank 23rd out of 25 Novembers, at 0.09 times the usual value for the same days in earlier years. Below that, the user sees: a burning calendar with one row per year; what usually happens in the next three months (this is history, not a forecast); this month compared with the same month in every earlier year; whether burning is rising or falling over the years; and a switch between the raw record and our corrected record. A user can pick a region, draw an area, type coordinates or search for a district, choose any dates, and download every chart as CSV, PNG and SVG. It works on a phone and needs no login. THE PROBLEM NASA has two kinds of fire sensors. The older one is MODIS. In 2012 a sharper one, VIIRS, joined it. VIIRS sees many more fires, so the raw count jumps about five times in 2012. The jump is the camera, not the fire. Because of this, the years before 2012 cannot be compared with today. HOW IT WORKS We fix two things separately. 1. The sharper camera counts one fire many times. We put a 1 km grid on the map and count each square only once per satellite pass. 2. The sharper camera sees weak fires that the older one misses. Where both satellites passed over the same place on the same day, we measured how often MODIS also saw a fire that VIIRS saw, for every fire strength. In Cordoba we count each VIIRS fire by its chance of being seen by MODIS. In Punjab and Haryana, where that measurement is weak, we count only fires above a fixed strength. Both are then scaled by one number for each calendar month. The weak fires that only VIIRS can see are not thrown away. They are kept as a separate layer. The raw jump in 2012 was about 5.2 times in Cordoba and 5.3 times in Punjab and Haryana. After our correction the step left is 0.066 in Cordoba and -0.020 in Punjab and Haryana (natural log), inside our limit of 0.10. HOW WE KNOW IT WORKS We wrote down ten checks and their pass marks before opening the data. Every result is shown in the app, including the ones that failed. Passed: the 2012 jump is gone in both main regions. A newer satellite, NOAA-20, which we never used to build the method, gives the same record (correlation 0.988 in Cordoba and 0.989 in Punjab and Haryana). The month-by-month check on years kept aside (2018 to 2019) passes in Cordoba (0.072 against a limit of 0.15) and just passes in Punjab and Haryana (0.148 against 0.15). Failed, and we say so: in Cordoba the method we ship fails one of our own checks, the 2016 check (-0.114 against a limit of 0.10). Our own rule said to ship the simpler method there. We chose the other one after seeing the results, because it is closer to MODIS month by month, and we say this openly. In Punjab and Haryana the check on 2020 to 2021 fails (0.169). The Chilecito area borrows Cordoba's settings and fails three checks. The Karnataka forest area was added late and passes none of its kept-aside checks, so a simple ratio is used there and the app labels it. We also found and fixed two of our own mistakes during the hackathon, and the page shows the corrected values. WHY IT MATTERS MODIS is ending. NASA plans to stop Terra's MODIS data in January 2027 and Aqua's around September 2027. Without a correction like this, every fire officer's history starts again in 2012. Fire Census keeps all the years on one scale and continues on VIIRS when MODIS ends. Fire teams, forest departments, pollution boards, land managers and researchers can all use it. WHAT IT DOES NOT DO It counts what satellites detected, not every fire. Fires under cloud or smoke are missed. The unit is 'Aqua-equivalent fire cells', not fires or hectares. It is set up for four study areas only. A single month can be off by about 7 percent in Cordoba and 16 percent in Punjab and Haryana in a typical month, and more in some months. It is not a forecast. It does not update by itself. HOW WE USED AI Claude (Anthropic) wrote most of the code under our direction: the data pipeline, the checks and the web app. It also drafted most of the documents and this page, and suggested possible methods and pass marks. The team chose the challenge, the regions and the method, fixed the checks before the data was opened, obtained the data from NASA, reviewed the results and made each decision. Every AI-assisted file says so in its first line, and docs/AI_USE.md in the repository lists each contribution. No AI-generated images, video or audio are in the project. TOOLS Data work: Python with DuckDB, pandas, PyArrow, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and matplotlib. Website: React, TypeScript and Vite, MapLibre GL JS over NASA GIBS imagery, and Observable Plot for charts. Hosting: GitHub Pages. Code: https://github.com/Mahabu-Subhani/fire-census WHY 9.9 MEGAWATT (THE MATHS) Fire strength is measured in megawatts (MW). It is called fire radiative power. MODIS has big pixels, so it often misses weak fires. For every fire strength we worked out one fraction: the VIIRS fires that MODIS also saw, divided by all the VIIRS fires, using places where both satellites passed on the same day. Plotted against fire strength, this gives a curve. It starts near 0 for weak fires and rises to a flat top for strong fires. The strength where the curve reaches half of its flat top is the midpoint. In Cordoba, in daytime, the midpoint is 9.9 MW. When we resample the data it stays between 8.6 and 12.3 MW. We then checked this number against a research paper that we did not use to build it. Sofiev and Kouznetsov (2026, Geoscientific Model Development) say that MODIS's daytime detection limit grows with pixel size: limit = 4.44 MW for each square km of pixel + 0.52 MW. The average Aqua pixel over Cordoba is 2.23 square km. So the limit is 4.44 x 2.23 + 0.52 = 10.4 MW. Our measured 9.9 MW and the paper's 10.4 MW are within about 5 percent of each other. We only counted when two satellites agreed, the paper started from the physics of the sensor, and both reach nearly the same number. That is why the curve is not a black box. In Punjab and Haryana the curve is weak, so the 4.8 MW cut-off there is a working choice, not a measured limit. IMPACT: PEOPLE NEAR FIRES We joined the fire record to the WorldPop 2020 population map. Every square of about 11 km gets a burning level from its fire detections in a year (light 1 to 9, moderate 10 to 49, heavy 50 or more), and the app counts how many people live in each level. The map can also be coloured by exposure, to show where heavy burning and dense population meet. This is where the harmonized record matters most: on the raw record the number of people living with heavy burning appears to jump in 2012 only because the new satellite sees more fires. A wrong record would point help to the wrong places and the wrong years. Limits: this is exposure, not harm or risk; one population map (2020) is used for every year; 'near' means living in the same square. ACCESSIBLE TO EVERYONE The calendar's colours were chosen and checked so that people with colour blindness can read them. Nothing depends on colour alone: months that are not harmonized are marked with a hatch pattern, the current month has an outline, every box shows its exact value on hover or tap, and every value is also given as a table. The app works on a phone, needs no login and no payment, and every chart can be downloaded as CSV, PNG or SVG.
